transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Ramos (Redwood Platform), Samir Patel (Atlas CTO), Laura Chen (Atlas SRE), Marcus King (Atlas ML Eng), Ivy Morales (Atlas Infra)

Summary: quick hit technical deep dive to triage p95/p99 jitter observed over last two weeks, compare streaming vs non-streaming behavior, check KV cache hotkey patterns, and surface potential network-hop induced stalls for Atlas's VPC-based private deployment. Agreed next step is a Redwood-run p99 lab + Atlas will share histograms and a traffic replay.

Topics: p95/p99, streaming vs non-streaming, batching, KV cache hotkeys, quantization profiles (int8/int4), network hops and Envoy sidecar, NFS/S3 weight fetch cold starts, VPC peering microbursts.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. we got the notes from Laura and Marcus about spikes. want to make this hands on if that's cool.
[00:25] Samir: yeah, our product hits a hard p99 requirement for interactive triage flows, and lately we're seeing 200-600ms spikes on p99 even when p95 is fine. it's making our on-call nervous.
[00:38] Priya: ok thanks. first, can you confirm streaming vs non-streaming percentage? streaming because that changes tail character.
[00:52] Marcus: roughly 40% streaming websocket partial tokens for the clinician assistant, 60% non-streaming sync text for batch summarization. the streaming ones show more jitter.
[01:05] Priya: good, that aligns with typical streaming tail exposure. streaming introduces more small-window writes and more backpressure sensitivity.
[01:20] Laura: we also saw some correlation with deployments in us-east-2 VPC when there's cross-account peering to our analytics cluster. not sure if that's a network hop issue or a runtime jitter.
[01:33] Ethan: quick hypothesis list i put together: kernel scheduling/CPU steal on the host, envoy sidecar queues, TCP Nagle/TCP_NODELAY misconfig, gRPC windowing behavior, KV cache hotkey contention, and cold model weight pulls from NFS/S3. we should test each systematically.

[02:05] [Jordan shares screen: latency heatmap slide]
[02:15] Jordan: this is the p95/p99 heatmap you sent in — notice p95 sits ~120ms while p99 jumps to 420ms in short bursts. those bursts line up with an increased 95th percentile for response size, but not always.
[02:32] Marcus: also some of the worst p99 hits happen for short prompts, which was surprising. we'd expect long prompts to cause larger tails.
[02:45] Priya: short prompts causing tail usually point to network or RPC stalls — e.g. TLS handshake renegotiation, or envoy queuing before the runtime actually sees tokens.
[03:00] Laura: our envoy config uses per-service thread pools; i can share. we do keepalives but maybe TLS session reuse isn't happening for all flows.
[03:12] Priya: good. please include envoy metrics for pending_requests, queue_length, and connection_reuse in the export.

[03:30] Samir: can you walk through how Redwood's runtime handles streaming vs non-streaming for tail mitigation?
[03:40] Priya: sure. at a high level: streaming opens a persistent RPC (gRPC or WS), tokens are emitted as they are decoded. streaming trades off early token emission vs throughput batching. to keep tail low we use continuous batching with small micro-batches for streaming and prefix/KV cache lookups to avoid recomputation. but streaming is sensitive to any per-request blocking I/O because it holds the connection open while waiting for more bytes.
[04:10] Priya: non-streaming runs allow the server to buffer more and pack larger batches which amortize kernel launch/overheads. that often reduces p99 for throughput-bound workloads, but increases p95 for single-user low-latency needs if batching delay is introduced.

[04:40] Marcus: what about quantization? we're running an int8-ish profile in staging. could quantization cause tail spikes?
[04:50] Ethan: quantization itself usually reduces latency, but mixed kernels or fallback codepaths can add jitter. for example, if an operator goes down a fallback to CPU or a slower kernel because an optimized kernel isn't available for a specific sequence length or attention pattern, you'll see outliers. also GPU memory fragmentation during dynamic batching can cause small allocation delays.
[05:20] Priya: exactly — we maintain small kernel selectors per model variant; mismatch between model config (e.g., rotary emb dims, grouped attention) and the compiled kernel can trigger slower paths. we should check model variant vs compiled artifact matching on Atlas's dedicated nodes.

[05:40] [06:00] Laura: Ivy, anything from infra?
[06:05] Ivy: we saw occasional MIG tenant eviction warnings on nights where other workloads are noisy. also the nodes are on a mixed NUMA layout; we haven't pinned processes. could that add p99 noise?
[06:20] Priya: yes, NUMA and CPU pinning matter — syscalls to allocate pinned pages across NUMA boundaries can add latency. also if gpu-to-cpu transfers are traversing an unexpected PCIe root-port due to numa locality, you'll see spikes.
[06:38] Jordan: ok, let's prioritize: (1) network hop mapping, (2) envoy queue/reuse, (3) kernel mismatch evidence, (4) KV hotkeys.

[06:50] [07:10] Marcus: about KV cache — we're using shared redis with grouping. are there hotkeys possible? our prompts often share a patient prefix so i suspect high k-v reads for the same prefix.
[07:25] Priya: common pattern: hot prefixes cause redis CPU saturation or single-instance contention, which serializes cache hits and pushes requests back to origin, adding tail latency. Redwood supports local LRU sharding in the runtime to avoid remote hotkey amplification. do you have cache hit ratios?
[07:45] Marcus: we have cache hits reported at 72% but the distribution is skewed — the top 2% of keys are 30% of cache hits.
[07:55] Ethan: that's a red flag. consider either client-side sharding for the hotkeys, or enable runtime-local cache for prefixes (we can enable a per-worker in-memory cache) to eliminate the round-trip for hot prefixes.

[08:20] Laura: are there concerns about cache consistency if we do local LRU? our product sometimes updates patient metadata mid-session.
[08:30] Priya: for short-lived session prefixes it's safe; for mutable state we either put a short TTL (500-2k ms) or use invalidation on write via a light pub/sub. for your use-case, a 1s TTL on prefix cache cuts tail but preserves correctness for most workflows.

[09:00] [09:25] Samir: network microbursts — do you have experience with VPC peering and intermittent 200–300ms blips caused by retransmits on short-lived connections?
[09:37] Jordan: yes, especially when TCP connections are created per request. moving to connection re-use or an HTTP/2/gRPC multiplexed connection reduces tail dramatically. also turning on TCP_NODELAY for small streaming frames helps.
[09:55] Priya: in addition check client TCP stack: socket buffer sizes, keepalive timeouts, and also avoid closing connections after each request. when clients open and close TLS frequently, the handshake jitter shows up on p99.

[10:20] Marcus: we use a fronting API gateway that terminates TLS and uses Envoy to talk to the runtime over mTLS. how many hops is too many?
[10:32] Ethan: each Envoy hop adds queueing and potential serialization. 2 hops is common (gateway envoy + sidecar envoy) — beyond that you start to observe compounded queuing. also check whether any of the envoys are doing request->span sampling logic that blocks.
[10:50] Laura: i can map the hop count and point out which subnets cross peering links.

[11:05] [11:20] Priya: let's talk about streaming vs non-streaming experiments: we'll run a repro with your seq length distribution and traffic shape. test matrix: streaming continuous micro-batches (max batch 4, micro-batch 8ms), streaming with per-request flush, non-streaming batching (max batch 64, 10ms aggregation), and non-streaming unbatched. measure p50/p95/p99 and 99.9.
[11:45] Jordan: we should also toggle quantization profiles during the lab — int8 vs int4 fallback to int8 — and intentionally force a kernel mismatch to see the outlier signature.

[12:00] Marcus: what are signatures of kernel fallback in metrics?
[12:08] Priya: you'll see a small population of requests with higher device-side latency and a spike in device context-switch metrics; on the host you'll also see elevated cudaMalloc/cudaFree calls if allocations aren't cached. Redwood exposes a kernel_path tag on spans so we can filter requests that used the slow path.

[12:30] [13:00] Laura: storage — we're using S3 for models and a warm local cache. could cold pulls affect p99? we did observe occasional pulls after node restarts.
[13:14] Ethan: a cold weight pull is very expensive — tens to hundreds of ms depending on bandwidth. runtime pre-warm and pinned model residency prevent that. check your node auto-scale policy: if nodes are scaling down aggressively you may get cold-starts on scale-up.
[13:36] Ivy: we have aggressive scale-down during nights. maybe that's aligning with some of the p99 windows.
[13:47] Priya: if you need strict p99 SLAs, consider reserved capacity (dedicated) so models stay resident. for a hybrid approach, allow a small burst buffer or keep one warm node per AZ.

[14:10] Jordan: another small item — protocol framing. our streaming currently uses websocket text frames for early prototyping; switching to binary gRPC streaming with smaller frame overhead improved p99 in other customers.
[14:25] Marcus: interesting — we picked websocket for simplicity, but switching might be okay.

[14:36] [15:00] Samir: what's the expected delta between streaming tuned vs non-streaming tuned p99?
[15:08] Priya: depends, but in practice streaming tuned (micro-batch + local cache + persistent connections) can cut p99 by 40–70% relative to naive streaming. non-streaming batching optimized for throughput can have lower p95 but sometimes a slightly higher p50 due to batching delay. those are heuristics — we need your traffic to be precise.

[15:40] Laura: do you recommend any quick Envoy config changes we can test?
[15:48] Priya: yes: enable connection pooling and keepalive, increase upstream buffer limits, set per-route max pending requests appropriately, and make sure health-checks aren't doing heavy work. also ensure Envoy access logs aren't sync-blocking.

[16:10] Marcus: and from Redwood side, what telemetry will you add in the lab?
[16:18] Jordan: we'll log per-request kernel_path, cache_hit boolean, batch_size, sequence_length, device_lat_ms, host_wait_ms, and network_hop_count where possible. we'll produce waterfall spans so you can see where time is spent.

[16:35] [17:00] Samir: security question — if we enable local runtime caches, any concerns about PHI residency?
[17:10] Priya: local caches are ephemeral and time-limited; we can encrypt at-rest and in-memory. most customers with PHI use short TTLs (<=1s) and retention controls. your compliance folks may want an explicit audit log for cache writes/evicts; Redwood can enable that.

[17:30] Ethan: one more subtle item: p99 can be caused by host-level cron jobs, logrotate, or backup tasks that temporarily throttle IO. do you have nightly cron alignment with your spikes?
[17:45] Laura: yes we do backups at 03:00 and sometimes cluster housekeeping triggers around 03:15 — but our worst p99 windows were midday.

[18:00] Priya: ok, so not just cron. still worth reviewing k8s eviction thresholds; kubelet OOM/rotate events can cause transient CPU steal.

[18:20] [18:45] Jordan: to recap — agreed Redwood lab to run streaming vs non-streaming matrix, toggle quantization profiles, force kernel fallback, measure KV hotkey effects with and without local cache, and map network hops + envoy metrics. Atlas will share traffic replay + histograms + envoy config.

[19:05] Samir: timeline acceptable. we'd like pilot week for on-prem deployment in late September.
[19:15] Jordan: noted — we'll propose dates after the lab results.

[19:30] [19:50] Laura: one last ask — can you include a short checklist for SRE to reduce tail quickly? e.g. keepalives, connection reuse, local cache toggle, reserved capacity sizing?
[19:58] Priya: yes we'll drop a one-page SRE quickfix doc.

[20:10] [20:30] Jordan: any other questions?
[20:35] Marcus: for the lab, please include a run where we intentionally add a 2-3ms synthetic RTT per hop to emulate peering microbursts so we can see compounding effects.
[20:48] Priya: yes we'll add that.

[21:00] Ethan: action items and next steps are in the meeting note. I'll also add a suggested kernel diagnostic script to collect cuda tracepoints during the lab.

[21:20] Samir: thanks all. happy if this reduces our p99 enough to avoid dedicated infra right away.
[21:30] Jordan: great — we'll follow up with the lab plan and calendar invites.

[21:40] Meeting end.

Notes about transcription quality: some proper nouns may be mis-transcribed (e.g., MIG evict -> 'migative', KV cache -> 'k v cash'), filler words retained.

References / Links mentioned: "latency heatmap" (shared in chat), "Envoy config snippet" (customer to share), "Redwood p99 lab runbook" (Redwood to share), SRE quickfix one-pager (to be provided).
